title: BLISS: A Billion scale Index using Iterative Re-partitioning

problem.claim: Information retrieval requires approximate nearest-neighbor search in high-dimensional vector spaces, while retrieval engines must balance latency, accuracy, scalability, compactness, and distributed load balancing under limited hardware and time-critical queries.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies a need for an indexing approach that improves these trade-offs and scales to billions of vectors.

contributions.claim: BLISS is a tunable indexing algorithm that iteratively learns query-relevant item buckets and uses the power-of-K choices strategy to balance them.
BLISS provides superior load balancing with high probability under benign assumptions.
BLISS supports both near-neighbor retrieval and extreme classification and is data- and model-parallel for distributed training and inference.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly propose BLISS as a new algorithm.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On four billion-vector ANN datasets, BLISS was compared with HNSW and FAISS on recall, inference time, indexing time, and index size.

Compared with HNSW, BLISS reportedly used 100x less RAM and achieved similar inference time at the same recall; compared with FAISS-IVF, it reportedly achieved similar performance with 3-4x less memory.
On popular extreme-classification datasets with half a million classes, BLISS reportedly exceeded the best baselines' precision and was 5x faster for inference.

narrative_sequence.summary: Representation learning frames information retrieval as approximate nearest-neighbor search in high-dimensional vector spaces, with competing operational requirements.
The authors propose BLISS, which learns relevant buckets iteratively and balances them using the power-of-K choices strategy.
BLISS is reported to provide high-probability load balancing and to support both ANN and XML workloads.
For ANN, the authors evaluate billion-vector datasets against HNSW and FAISS, reporting lower memory requirements and comparable performance.
For XML, the authors report higher precision and faster inference than the best baselines on multi-label datasets with half a million classes.

source_observation.claim: BLISS learns query-relevant buckets from query-item relevance data and iteratively refines its partitions.

interpretation.claim: Partitioning informed directly by task relevance may improve the trade-off between search quality and index efficiency.

application.claim: Use relevance-aware iterative partitioning when designing large-scale retrieval or classification indexes.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how performance changes across data distributions, relevance-label quality, or assumptions beyond describing them as benign.

source_observation.claim: BLISS reportedly reduces memory requirements substantially while maintaining similar or better reported task performance.

interpretation.claim: Index compactness can be a primary scaling lever when memory limits constrain billion-scale retrieval.

application.claim: Evaluate large-scale indexes jointly on quality, latency, indexing cost, and memory footprint.

exception.claim: The abstract does not provide absolute latency, indexing-time, hardware, or statistical-evaluation details.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, hardware configurations, parameter settings, or absolute metric values.
The abstract does not describe the benign assumptions underlying the load-balancing guarantee.
The abstract does not provide implementation details or reproducibility information.
